labelChecks.title: Test psyllium before baking with it
labelChecks.text: Psyllium is on your not-tried list, and psyllium allergy does happen (mostly from breathing in the powder). Given your anaphylaxis history, check with your allergist first. For a first try, stir a small amount (well under a teaspoon) into a full glass of water and drink it right away, then watch how you feel. Pour the powder gently so you don't breathe it in. If it goes fine, mark it in Allergy Swipe. Terrasoul says its psyllium is packed in a facility that also processes tree nuts.

labelChecks.title: Baking powder must be corn-free
labelChecks.text: Most baking powder (Rumford, Clabber Girl, Bob's Red Mill) contains cornstarch. Use Hain Featherweight (monocalcium phosphate, potato starch, potassium bicarbonate). Hain doesn't guarantee against corn cross-contact. It starts reacting as soon as it gets wet, so bake right after it goes in.

labelChecks.title: Plain salt, no dextrose
labelChecks.text: Iodized salt often contains dextrose, which is usually made from corn. Use plain, non-iodized salt or sea salt with nothing else on the label.

labelChecks.title: Grind whole chia yourself
labelChecks.text: Pre-ground chia can share equipment with flax or nuts. Buy whole chia and grind it in a spice or coffee grinder.

labelChecks.title: Honey over maple; cane sugar
labelChecks.text: Maple producers sometimes use an unlabeled defoamer, which can be sunflower or canola oil. Use honey, or ask the producer. Plain "sugar" can be beet sugar, so buy one labeled cane sugar.

labelChecks.title: Extra virgin olive oil
labelChecks.text: "Light" or "pure" olive oil can be blended. Extra virgin is a single ingredient. Don't use cooking spray; it often has soy lecithin or canola.

labelChecks.title: Ask flour makers about sesame
labelChecks.text: Rice flours and starches are often milled near sesame, nuts, or dairy. Bob's Red Mill's gluten-free facility handles sesame, so skip it. The Amazon picks below favor dedicated facilities, but email the brand to confirm before the first purchase.

recipes.title: Rice sub rolls
recipes.summary: Soft, slightly chewy sub-style rolls with no yeast, eggs, or gums. Psyllium gives them bread-like structure, and baking with steam gives them a thin crust.

items.note: Helps keep psyllium from tinting the bread purple.

items.item: Sheet pan, parchment, and a metal (not glass) pan for steam

steps.text: First time only: test psyllium on its own before baking with it (see the label checks below), then mark it in Allergy Swipe.
Put a metal baking pan on the lowest oven rack and heat the oven to 450°F. Line a sheet pan with parchment. Bring a kettle of water to a boil.
Whisk all the dry ingredients together, including the baking powder and soda.

In another bowl, whisk the psyllium into the warm water, oil, honey, vinegar, and lemon juice. Whisk fast; it turns into thick jelly within a minute or two. That's normal. Go straight to the next step so it doesn't set too firm to mix in.

Add the gel to the dry ingredients. Mix with a spatula, then your hands, just until a soft, slightly tacky dough forms (about 30 seconds). Don't overwork it; the baking powder is already working, so keep moving.

With wet hands, divide the dough into 4. Shape each into a log about 7 inches long and 2 inches wide, keeping it tall rather than flat, since it spreads. Space them 2 inches apart. Brush with water and cut 3–4 shallow diagonal slashes on top.
Slide the rolls in. Carefully pour about 1 cup of boiling water into the hot pan below (stand back from the steam), close the door, and turn the oven down to 425°F. Bake 20 minutes.

Take out the water pan, lower the oven to 400°F, and bake 10–15 minutes more, until golden and the center of a roll reads 205–210°F. Without a thermometer: the bottom sounds hollow when tapped and the roll feels light.
Cool on a rack at least 1 hour before slicing; psyllium bread finishes setting as it cools. Split lengthwise for subs.

tips: Weigh the flours if you can. If you use cups, spoon the flour into the cup and level it off; scooping straight from the bag packs in extra flour and makes it dense.
If the rolls spread flat, use 20 g less water next time. If the middle is gummy, bake longer, to temperature.
A purple or grey tint is harmless and comes from some psyllium brands. Try another brand if it bothers you.
Freeze extras and toast or warm them before eating.
Untested recipe, built from published yeast-free psyllium rolls. Expect to adjust after the first batch.

recipes.title: Banana bread
recipes.summary: Moist, tender banana bread from rice and almond flour, bound with chia. Grew out of the first loaf, which came out more like cake than bread.

items.note: Helps it hold together; fine to leave out.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 350°F. Line the loaf pan with a parchment sling and rub a little oil on the short ends.

Mash the bananas well. Whisk in the ground chia and its water right away (don't let the chia gel on its own first, or it clumps), then whisk in the sugar, oil, and vinegar. Let it sit while you measure the dry ingredients.
Whisk the dry ingredients in another bowl, then fold them into the banana mix just until no dry flour shows.
Scrape into the pan and smooth the top. Bake 60–70 minutes, laying foil loosely over the top once it's well browned (around 35 minutes), until the center reads 205–210°F.
Rest 15 minutes in the pan, lift out by the parchment, and cool on a rack at least 2 hours before slicing.

tips: Weigh the flours if you can. If you use cups, spoon the flour into the cup and level it off; scooping straight from the bag packs in extra flour and makes it dense.
The browner the bananas, the sweeter and moister the bread.
Blueberries or chopped dates are good stir-ins. Skip chocolate chips unless you've checked them for dairy.
Slice and freeze; toast slices straight from frozen.

recipes.title: Rice pancake mix
recipes.summary: A jar mix of white rice flour, tapioca, and chia. Add water and oil for a batch of egg-free, dairy-free pancakes.
recipes.yield: About 4 batches; each batch makes about 8 pancakes

items.item: Lard or olive oil for the pan
Mashed ripe banana (use 180 g / ¾ cup water instead)

steps.text: Whisk the dry mix together well so the baking powder and chia are spread evenly. Store it airtight. Stir or shake the jar before each scoop, since it settles.
Heat a skillet over medium heat. Whisk one batch of mix with the water, oil, and vinegar (and banana, if using). Let it sit a few minutes while the pan heats; it will thicken.

Grease the pan lightly. Pour about ¼ cup batter per pancake. Flip gently when bubbles pop on top and the edges look dry, then cook the other side until golden. Keep them small; rice pancakes are tender.

tips: If the middles stay gummy, turn the heat down a little and cook longer.
Top with honey and fruit. Skip butter and most syrups unless the label checks out.

storeBought.title: 1-2-3 Gluten Free “Allie's Awesome Buckwheat Pancakes”
storeBought.text: Still sold. The ingredient list we found is from an older box, so check the current one. Make it with water and a chia egg (1 Tbsp ground chia + 3 Tbsp water) instead of egg and milk.
storeBought.ask: Before using: call 1-2-3 Gluten Free (440-264-3920) and ask whether the sugar is cane or beet, what carrier the added vitamins use (often corn), and whether sesame, dairy, or fish run on the same lines.

items.item: Corn-free baking powder (sodium acid pyrophosphate, baking soda, tapioca starch, monocalcium phosphate)
Niacin, reduced iron, calcium carbonate, thiamin, folic acid, riboflavin
